feature extractors like FasterRCNN with lightweight Shuf-

1. Introduction
Deep neural networks have elevated the capability of ma-
chines for image understanding and natural language mod-
eling. Automatic Image Captioning (AIC) is a research area
that enables machines to automatically generate meaningful
textual descriptions for input images. This capability is es-
sential for multimodal AI applications, including assistive
technologies for visually impaired individuals, intelligent
human-machine interfaces, and visual content retrieval [1].
However, despite significant advancements in image cap-
tioning research [2, 3, 4, 5, 6], the practical deployment
of the state-of-art models remain a major challenge. This
can be attributed to the prioritization of achieving arbitrar-
ily high overall accuracy at the cost of computational effi-
ciency. This often renders most models unsuitable for cer-
tain real-world applications that require on-device process-
ing and low-latency inference on energy-efficient edge de-
vices.
Early image captioning models have used template-
based and retrieval-based approaches to generate captions.
These early approaches have either filled blank spaces in a
fixed sentence template or retrieved similar captions from
a prefix caption database. Though these approaches were
simple, the generated captions were of fixed size, or the
captions were often irrelevant to image content. The in-
troduction of deep learning-based image captioning models
could mitigate these issues up to some extent [7]. The deep
learning-based models mainly consist of three main compo-
nents – (a) Visual Feature Encoder, (b) Visual Feature Re-
finer, and (c) Decoder With Attention (see Figure 1). These
models [2, 3, 4, 5, 6] have achieved impressive performance
by leveraging computation-heavy visual feature extractors.
However, these advancements came with a significant in-
crease in computational demands and memory footprint.

Due to the transformer-based architectures, the compu-
tational requirements for the ORT [6] model surpassed oth-
ers. The high computational demand and large parameter
counts made it infeasible for real-time caption generation on
resource-constrained devices such as smartphones, tablets,
and embedded AI systems. These high computational costs
not only hinder on-device deployment but also increase re-
liance on cloud-based inference, leading to latency issues
and higher energy consumption. Such dependencies create
accessibility barriers, particularly in remote areas where in-
ternet connectivity is unreliable. This observation motivates
the present work to develop a lightweight image captioning
model by utilizing lightweight CNNs as visual feature en-
coders.
Most image captioning research has been centered
around high-resource languages such as English, Chi-
nese [10], and German [11], while low-resource languages
like Assamese have received minimal attention. The As-
samese language is the official language of the North-East
Indian state of Assam. It is an Indo-Aryan language simi-
lar to Hindi, Bengali, and Oriya. The Assamese language
follows a left-to-right writing script similar to the Bengali
language.
Assamese is a morphologically rich language
with complex grammar having inflection, gender and tense
markers. Additionally, Assamese has 15.31 million native
speakers, out of which 85% reside in rural areas and are
more fluent in Assamese than English. A lightweight As-
samese image captioning system for edge devices could ad-
dress real-world challenges. An AI-based assistive technol-
ogy using Assamese image captioning can help 0.3% of the
population of Assam who suffer from visual impairment .
Moreover, 70% of students from Assam get their elemen-
tary education in the Assamese language . Therefore, a
computationally efficient Assamese captioning model can
help in smart education technology for language learn-
ing [12]. The design of image captioning models with lower
computations and parameters is vital for such practical ap-
plications.
This is particularly applicable for other low-
resource languages as well for broader accessibility and us-
ability of AI systems.
While deep learning-based image captioning models
have achieved remarkable success, their adoption in real-
world applications remains constrained by high computa-
tional demands and hardware limitations. Most state-of-
the-art models prioritize performance, often at the expense
of efficiency, making them impractical for deployment on
edge devices. This limitation is particularly evident in ap-
plications like assistive technologies for visually impaired
individuals, where computational efficiency is crucial for
real-time operation. To address these challenges, this work
introduces AC-Lite, a lightweight image captioning model
for low-resource Assamese language. AC-Lite is designed
for deployment on computation resource-constrained de-
vices (e.g. smartphones). Additionally, the model should
operate smoothly on the device hardware without connect-
ing to any remote server for caption generation. To achieve
this, the proposed AC-Lite model uses computationally ef-
ficient CNN models for the visual feature encoder. Addi-
tionally, the Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) have been em-
ployed in the decoder due to their fewer parameters, fewer

ther, bilinear attention [13] is also employed with the pro-
posed AC-Lite to boost the performance. Moreover, a rein-
forcement learning-based approach [14] is applied for fur-
ther improvement of captioning performance. The perfor-
mance of AC-Lite is evaluated by using COCO-Assamese
Caption (COCO-AC) and the Flickr30K-Assamese Caption
(Flickr30K-AC) datasets proposed in [13]. The major con-
tributions of this work are as follows.
• Development of AC-Lite, a computationally efficient
lightweight image captioning model for the Assamese
language.
• Exploration of different lightweight Convolutional
Neural Networks as an alternative to FasterRCNN for
visual feature encoding.
• A GRU-based caption decoder with bilinear attention
is employed to achieve better performance with less
computational requirement. The model performance
is further enhanced using reinforcement learning.
2. Related Work
The state-of-art image captioning models adopted the
encoder-decoder based deep learning framework [7] from
neural machine translation (NMT). In NMT, an RNN en-
codes the input word sequence, and another RNN is used as
the decoder to generate the target word sequence. Vinyals
et al. [3] used GoogleNet [8] for visual feature encoding
and long short-term memory (LSTM) network for caption
generation. The visual features are only used as the ini-
tial hidden state for the LSTM network. However, the vi-
sual features weaken over long sequences due to the van-
ishing gradient problem. Xu et al. [2] addressed this issue
through the introduction of a visual attention mechanism
where attended features are fed to the LSTM at each decod-
ing step. Anderson et al. [4] employed FasterRCNN [9] for
extracting visual features from salient regions (bottom-up
features) to focus on important scene objects. Subsequent
works [5, 16] reported further performance improvement
using these bottom-up features. Huang et al. [5] incorpo-
rated multi-head self-attention to refine the visual features
and combined them with LSTM for caption generation.
Transformer architectures have improved image cap-
tioning performance by visual feature refinement and by
enhancing the semantic accuracy of captions.
Cornia et
al. [15] proposed a meshed-memory transformer, linking
encoder and decoder layers for multi-level vision-language
relationships, with a memory-augmented attention mech-
anism.
Pan et al. [16] introduced X-linear attention in
transformers, enabling second-order interactions for richer
representations.
Herdade et al. [6] adjusted attention
weights using geometric shapes and spatial positions. Nair
et al. [17] replaced trigonometric positional embeddings
with spatial positions of salient regions. However, these
transformer-based architectures are quite computation in-
tensive and cannot be deployed on edge devices (see Ta-
ble 1).
Lightweight Convolutional Neural Networks have gained
popularity for their operational efficiency on computa-
tion resource-constrained devices.
For instance, Mo-
bileNetV1 [18] and MobileNetV2 [19] used techniques
like depth-wise separable convolutions and inverted bottle-
neck blocks for reducing computations.
Following that,
other lightweight CNNs like ShuffleNetV1 [29], Shuf-
fleNetV2 [21], EfficientNet [22], and MobileNetV3 [20]
emerged. These lightweight CNNs also have scaled-down
versions like ShuffleNetV2X0.5, ShuffleNetV2X1.0, Shuf-
fleNetV2X1.5, ShuffleNetV2X2.0 and MobileNetv3 small
which operate in different configurations. However, these
CNNs favor speed over accuracy, leading to slightly re-
duced performance.
Lightweight Image Captioning models focus on ef-
ficiency for resource-constrained settings.
Models like
ACORT [25] and COMIC [30] used parameter and vocab-
ulary size reduction techniques. ACORT [25] reduced pa-
rameters through cross-layer and attention parameter shar-
ing, achieving a 13× reduction compared to transform-
ers [31]. Additionally, the authors introduced Radix En-
coding to minimize vocabulary size.
The Radix Encod-
ing method encodes the original vocabulary into a smaller
set of symbols, thus reducing the parameter count in
the embedding matrix.
COMIC [30] employed a simi-
lar vocabulary encoding technique to reduce parameters.
LCM-Captioner [23] used TextLighT to map visual fea-
tures to a lower-dimensional space. Zhang et al. substi-
tuted FasterRCNN with MobileNetV3 for visual encoding
and employed the transformer decoder for caption decod-
ing. LightCap [24] used pre-trained CLIP model for vi-
sual feature encoding without relying on resource-intensive
object detectors.
SMALLCAP [26] combined retrieval-
augmented generation with pre-trained CLIP vision encoder
and GPT-2, thereby reducing total trainable parameters. I-
Tuning [27] used cross-attention to link the frozen CLIP and
GPT-2 models, thus reducing trainable parameters by up to
10× while maintaining the overall performance.
Image Captioning in Indian Languages like Assamese,
Bengali, and Hindi is scarce, primarily due to the lack of
large-scale image-caption datasets. Mishra et al. [33] intro-
duced MSCOCO-Hindi by translating MSCOCO-English
captions into Hindi.
Additionally, the authors employ
ResNet101 [35] as visual feature encoder and GRU with
attention for caption generation. In another work, Mishra et
al. [32] used the transformer decoder with ResNet101 for
Hindi caption generation. In Assamese language, Nath et
al. [34] used a similar translation-based approach to create

Assamese image-caption dataset and employed Efficient-
NetB3 with GRU for caption generation. However, auto-
matically translated Assamese captions often suffer from
syntactic and semantic errors [13] and that is not addressed
in [34]. Choudhury et al. [13] addressed this issue by manu-
ally correcting the translation errors to develop the COCO-
Assamese and Flickr30K-Assamese datasets. Additionally,
the authors employed FasterRCNN for visual feature encod-
ing and Bi-LSTM with bilinear attention for caption gen-
eration. Further, Choudhury et al. [28] showed that mod-
els trained exclusively on Assamese image-caption datasets
outperform those trained on English datasets and subse-
quently translated into Assamese. This highlights the im-
portance of developing image caption datasets and models
for low-resource languages like Assamese.
3. Proposed Work
The proposed AC-Lite model consists of three main
components – (a) Visual Feature Encoder, (b) Bilinear At-
tention, and (c) Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) for caption
decoding as shown in Figure 2(a). AC-Lite uses pre-trained
CNNs (trained on ImageNet) as the visual feature encoder.
Initially, the Visual Feature Encoder takes an input image
and transforms it into a feature map of size da × nh × nw.
These feature maps are then flattened to create visual fea-
ture vectors A = [a1, . . . ai, . . . ana] (ai ∈Rda×1, A ∈
Rda×na, na = nh × nw). The extracted visual features A
are then fed to the Bilinear Attention module to generate the
attended visual feature ˆat at each decoding step t.

formance for Assamese image captioning task [13]. In the
original paper [13], the bilinear attention module consists
of an attention LSTM LSTMA and attention weight com-
putation mechanism. However, to reduce computation, we
replace LSTMA with a Gated Linear Unit (GRU) GRUA
as shown in Figure 2(b). At the tth decoding step, GRUA
produces a partial caption, and its context is captured in

consists of images from the Flickr30K-Main dataset with their

 these datasets and evaluated using the CIDEr score, which

for low-resource Assamese language. AC-Lite is designed
for deployment on computation resource-constrained de-
vices (e.g. smartphones). Additionally, the model should
operate smoothly on the device hardware without connect-
ing to any remote server for caption generation. To achieve
this, the proposed AC-Lite model uses computationally ef-
ficient CNN models for the visual feature encoder. Addi-
tionally, the Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) have been em-
ployed in the decoder due to their fewer parameters, fewer

• Exploration of different lightweight Convolutional

2. Related Work
The state-of-art image captioning models adopted the
encoder-decoder based deep learning framework [7] from
neural machine translation (NMT). In NMT, an RNN en-
codes the input word sequence, and another RNN is used as
the decoder to generate the target word sequence. Vinyals
et al. [3] used GoogleNet [8] for visual feature encoding
and long short-term memory (LSTM) network for caption
generation. The visual features are only used as the ini-
tial hidden state for the LSTM network. However, the vi-
sual features weaken over long sequences due to the van-
ishing gradient problem. Xu et al. [2] addressed this issue
through the introduction of a visual attention mechanism
where attended features are fed to the LSTM at each decod-
ing step. Anderson et al. [4] employed FasterRCNN [9] for
extracting visual features from salient regions (bottom-up
features) to focus on important scene objects. Subsequent
works [5, 16] reported further performance improvement
using these bottom-up features. Huang et al. [5] incorpo-
rated multi-head self-attention to refine the visual features
and combined them with LSTM for caption generation.
Transformer architectures have improved image cap-
tioning performance by visual feature refinement and by
enhancing the semantic accuracy of captions.
Cornia et
al. [15] proposed a meshed-memory transformer, linking
encoder and decoder layers for multi-level vision-language
relationships, with a memory-augmented attention mech-
anism.
Pan et al. [16] introduced X-linear attention in
transformers, enabling second-order interactions for richer
representations.
Herdade et al. [6] adjusted attention
weights using geometric shapes and spatial positions. Nair
et al. [17] replaced trigonometric positional embeddings
with spatial positions of salient regions. However, these
transformer-based architectures are quite computation in-
tensive and cannot be deployed on edge devices (see Ta-
ble 1).
Lightweight Convolutional Neural Networks have gained
popularity for their operational efficiency on computa-
tion resource-constrained devices.
For instance, Mo-
bileNetV1 [18] and MobileNetV2 [19] used techniques
like depth-wise separable convolutions and inverted bottle-
neck blocks for reducing computations.
Following that,
other lightweight CNNs like ShuffleNetV1 [29], Shuf-
fleNetV2 [21], EfficientNet [22], and MobileNetV3 [20]
emerged. These lightweight CNNs also have scaled-down
versions like ShuffleNetV2X0.5, ShuffleNetV2X1.0, Shuf-
fleNetV2X1.5, ShuffleNetV2X2.0 and MobileNetv3 small
which operate in different configurations. However, these
CNNs favor speed over accuracy, leading to slightly re-
duced performance.
Lightweight Image Captioning models focus on ef-
ficiency for resource-constrained settings.
Models like
ACORT [25] and COMIC [30] used parameter and vocab-
ulary size reduction techniques. ACORT [25] reduced pa-
rameters through cross-layer and attention parameter shar-
ing, achieving a 13× reduction compared to transform-
ers [31]. Additionally, the authors introduced Radix En-
coding to minimize vocabulary size.
The Radix Encod-
ing method encodes the original vocabulary into a smaller
set of symbols, thus reducing the parameter count in
the embedding matrix.
COMIC [30] employed a simi-
lar vocabulary encoding technique to reduce parameters.
LCM-Captioner [23] used TextLighT to map visual fea-
tures to a lower-dimensional space. Zhang et al. substi-
tuted FasterRCNN with MobileNetV3 for visual encoding
and employed the transformer decoder for caption decod-
ing. LightCap [24] used pre-trained CLIP model for vi-
sual feature encoding without relying on resource-intensive
object detectors.
SMALLCAP [26] combined retrieval-
augmented generation with pre-trained CLIP vision encoder
and GPT-2, thereby reducing total trainable parameters. I-
Tuning [27] used cross-attention to link the frozen CLIP and
GPT-2 models, thus reducing trainable parameters by up to
10× while maintaining the overall performance.
Image Captioning in Indian Languages like Assamese,
Bengali, and Hindi is scarce, primarily due to the lack of
large-scale image-caption datasets. Mishra et al. [33] intro-
duced MSCOCO-Hindi by translating MSCOCO-English
captions into Hindi.
Additionally, the authors employ
ResNet101 [35] as visual feature encoder and GRU with
attention for caption generation. In another work, Mishra et
al. [32] used the transformer decoder with ResNet101 for
Hindi caption generation. In Assamese language, Nath et
al. [34] used a similar translation-based approach to create

Assamese image-caption dataset and employed Efficient-
NetB3 with GRU for caption generation. However, auto-
matically translated Assamese captions often suffer from
syntactic and semantic errors [13] and that is not addressed
in [34]. Choudhury et al. [13] addressed this issue by manu-
ally correcting the translation errors to develop the COCO-
Assamese and Flickr30K-Assamese datasets. Additionally,
the authors employed FasterRCNN for visual feature encod-
ing and Bi-LSTM with bilinear attention for caption gen-
eration. Further, Choudhury et al. [28] showed that mod-
els trained exclusively on Assamese image-caption datasets
outperform those trained on English datasets and subse-
quently translated into Assamese. This highlights the im-
portance of developing image caption datasets and models
for low-resource languages like Assamese.
3. Proposed Work
The proposed AC-Lite model consists of three main
components – (a) Visual Feature Encoder, (b) Bilinear At-
tention, and (c) Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) for caption
decoding as shown in Figure 2(a). AC-Lite uses pre-trained
CNNs (trained on ImageNet) as the visual feature encoder.
Initially, the Visual Feature Encoder takes an input image
and transforms it into a feature map of size da × nh × nw.

replace LSTMA with a Gated Linear Unit (GRU) GRUA

4. Experimental Setup
The hyperparameters, dataset preparation methodology
and the baseline models are briefly described in this section.
4.1. Hyper Parameters
The visual feature encoder takes RGB images of size
3 × 224 × 224 as input and produces a feature map of size
1024 × 14 × 14. These features are extracted from the fi-
nal convolutional layers of the CNN. Later, adaptive pool-
ing transforms this feature map into na = 14 × 14 = 196
feature vectors of da = 1024 dimension. The GRU and at-
tention GRU hidden layer sizes are set to hG
t = hA
t = 512.
The attention embedding dimension is set to de = 512. The
model is trained by using Adam optimizer with a learning
rate of 5 × 10−4. The model is trained for 30 epochs with a
batch size of 50 image-caption pairs.
4.2. Dataset Preparation
The proposed model is trained and tested with COCO-
AC and Flickr30K-AC dataset. Initially, the dataset is pre-
processed to remove the punctuations and the captions are
truncated to a maximum of 16 tokens. Later, vocabulary
lists are created from the words that occurred more than five
times. This resulted in a vocabulary list of 12,912 words
for COCO-AC, and 8,534 words for Flickr30K-AC. The
COCO-AC and Flickr30K-AC dataset contains 123K and
31K images with five captions per image. The COCO-AC
dataset is divided into 113K images for training and 5K
each for testing and validation. For Flickr30K-AC, this di-
vision is 29K for training and 1K each for testing and val-
idation.

Baseline-4: The Baseline-4 employs the Object Relation

features adjust attention weights and improve the ability of
the model to capture spatial relationships within images for
more accurate caption generation.
Baseline-5: The Baseline-5 employs the Attention on At-

refinement and with the LSTM decoder for caption genera-
tion.
Baseline-6: The Baseline-6 employs a Bi-LSTM network
with Bilinear Attention [13]. The Bi-LSTM captures se-
quential dependencies in both forward and backward direc-
tions which is important for capturing the linguistic prop-
erties of Assamese language. Additionally, the bilinear at-
tention applies second-order interactions to improve model
performance.
5. Results and Discussion
The quantitative performance analysis, ablation studies
and qualitative results are presented in this section.
5.1. Quantitative Results
The quantitative results are obtained by using beam sizes
of 6 and 3 for COCO-AC and Flickr30K-AC, respectively.
The Table 2 and Table 3 compare the performance of the
proposed AC-Lite model with the existing Assamese image
captioning model and baseline models. The AC-Lite model
trained with cross-entropy loss (AC-Lite + XE) achieves
respective BLEU-1, BLEU-4, and CIDEr scores of 63.6,
24.1, and 72 on COCO-AC, and 54.9, 16.6, and 40.0 on
Flickr30K-AC, with only 1097.57 MFLOPs and 25.65M
parameters. Compared to Baseline-5 and Baseline-6, the
performance of the AC-Lite model is slightly lower. How-
ever, the computation requirement is 110× lower than state-
of-art Assamese captioning models. Moreover, when the
proposed model is trained with reinforcement learning (AC-
Lite + RL), it outperforms all other models, achieving 68.3
BLEU-1, 26 BLEU-4, and 82.3 CIDEr on COCO-AC. In
the case of Flickr30K-AC, the model trained with reinforce-
ment learning (AC-Lite + RL) gives competitive results
achieving 58.5 BLEU-1, 18.4 BLEU-4, and 46.1 CIDEr.
This impressive performance with less computation indi-
cates that the AC-Lite model is suitable for deployment in
resource-constrained environments.

ated captions can identify the color of the shirt as
(Orange) as well as activity
(Snowboarding) and

Additionally, in Fig-
ure 3(a), the proposed model can identify the environment
as
(Mountain) more accurately. The same can be

(Sidewalk) and

to the fact that the CNN models provide the whole image as

respectively.
6. Conclusion
This paper introduces AC-Lite, a lightweight image cap-
tioning model designed for the Assamese language. The
AC-Lite model is designed to meet the need for compu-
tationally efficient solutions that can operate on resource-
constrained devices. AC-Lite employs lightweight Shuf-
fleNetv2x1.5 for visual feature extraction and Gated Recur-
rent Units (GRUs) in the decoder. This incorporation sig-
nificantly reduces computational demands and model pa-
rameters.
Additionally, the integration of bilinear atten-
tion further enhances captioning performance. AC-Lite is
designed to function independently on device hardware,
thereby eliminating dependency on remote servers. This
makes it suitable for real-world applications like assistive
technologies and smart education technology for Assamese
speakers, particularly in rural areas. Future efforts will fo-
cus on improving semantic understanding and further opti-
mizing the model for enhanced performance in diverse real-
world scenarios.
